name: Emeka Dubois

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI firms. Your answers are confidential. What is a normal day at work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I clean up tracks at the youth centre, teach five beginner bass pupils and play a Saturday café set when we get the booking. I left school after secondary classes, and I am still learning the technical side; AI helps me label takes and make rough lesson exercises every day.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household depending on?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Lina works shifts at a care home, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. There are few similar music jobs around here and about two weeks of expenses in our account, so I check each centre booking.

say: I'd say **AI labels** save me a little time but do not bring paying listeners.
I'd ask the **youth centre** for confirmed blocks before planning the month.
think: Our **two-week reserve** makes one cancelled block a household problem.
Lina's **care home shifts** buy food, but they cannot reliably replace my pay.
do: Confirm next month's **two blocks** with the youth centre this week.
Keep my **five bass pupils** on their existing lesson slots.
Put **thirty** from a paid café set into the bills envelope.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the mortgage despite modest AI change.
S0.quote: A missed recording block can turn the school uniform money into the mortgage money.
fieldNote: His **daily AI use** saves time but does not solve irregular centre bookings.
A **two-week reserve** and school costs make him anxious before any large AI shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the youth centre that the software can label my takes faster, but it still cannot fill the Saturday room. I use AI every day for a rough set list, and that is a small help, not a new income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage already makes me check the account each morning. Lina's care home shifts cover food, but we have about two weeks of expenses saved and the youth centre gives me only monthly recording blocks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the centre to confirm next month's two recording blocks and keep my five beginner bass pupils on their slots. If the Saturday café set pays, I'll put thirty into a bills envelope before buying new strings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even when AI changes little. A missed recording block can turn the school uniform money into the mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened when the centre cancelled a block?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre cancelled a block in August and I used the children's school-clothes money for the mortgage. Lina picked up an extra care shift, but we cannot build a plan from that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at home needs to know what is booked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the centre administrator for dates by email, then tell Lina what actually booked. Our older child hears us talking about money, so I try to speak plainly without making a promise.

say: I'd ask for the centre's **paid-hour plan** in writing.
I'd compare **junior player invoices** with the local musicians group.
think: **Track cleaning and booking** could lose me half my centre pay.
I cannot assume **live bass work** will replace those hours at my current skill level.
do: Bring **eight invoices** to two players and the musicians group this month.
Ask about **care home kitchen shifts** if blocks halve and paid vacancies exist.
Keep **two centre blocks** if they remain on a written rota.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because half the recording schedule would threaten the mortgage.
S1.quote: Quick feet do not print a wage slip.
fieldNote: His **junior standing** makes a switch to better-paid live work uncertain.
He pairs **group questions** about lost hours with conditional care home work for income.

steps.text: Bring eight invoices to two players and musicians group
Ask care home about kitchen shifts if blocks halve and vacancies exist
Keep two centre blocks if written rota confirms them

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre manager that AI can draft the booking messages, but somebody must tell us which paid hours remain. I would ask other junior players to compare our shifts before accepting a new flat fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The centre pays me for cleaning tracks, lesson notes and booking calls, and that could all shrink. I am not the strongest bassist in town, so I cannot assume the live sets will replace half my weekly pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll collect the last eight centre invoices and ask two other players to bring theirs to the local musicians group. In the first year of the shift, if recording blocks drop from two to one monthly, I'll ask the care home about weekend kitchen shifts, but only if they have paid openings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because the mortgage has no room for a halved recording schedule. Quick feet do not print a wage slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the musicians group ask the manager?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We would ask for the new fee and block schedule in writing, not accuse the manager over a rumour. If the centre still offers two blocks, I would keep them and watch the invoices.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Can Lina actually find you extra shifts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lina can ask about care home vacancies, but her supervisor cannot invent a budget. I would not count those shifts until there is a rota and a rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre that AGI by 2028 means it must show us the hours plan before the next term. I would still play the café set while people keep paying to hear us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could edit audio, draft lessons and answer clients better and cheaper than I can. Robots that can play or handle instruments arrive around 2031, but the centre could cut my screen hours first, and Lina's wage alone will not carry the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask for a six-month block schedule and call the credit union about its mortgage hardship terms. In the first year after 2028, if one of my two monthly blocks disappears, I'll take paid kitchen shifts at the care home if a vacancy opens and keep my five pupils if families still book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, but not frozen. Two weeks of savings means I have to make the calls before a missed bill, not after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you accept the first mortgage relief offer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the credit union what extra interest a short payment break would cost. I would not sign a change until Lina and I see the full amount.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the care home has no vacancy?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A care home vacancy might take months; I know that. I'd ask the centre about any paid live setup shifts while waiting, but only if they do not clash with my pupils.

I'd tell my children a **certificate** is a chance, not a job offer.

fieldNote: His **five-year window** permits training if funding, childcare and venue acceptance align.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell junior musicians that five years is enough to train if a bursary pays, and I would use AI to practise. A certificate is a chance, not a job offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI could take centre editing and lesson notes in 2031, with robot players arriving around 2034. I might learn to run live sound and teach group sessions, but equipment work faces its own later robot risk and I still have a mortgage every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This winter I'll ask the adult college about a live sound certificate only if a bursary covers fees and evening classes fit the children's school routine. By 2031 I'll try to build paid setup shifts; in the first year after AGI, I'll apply to two venues for sound work if qualified and if they offer paid hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious rather than hopeful enough to relax. The time helps, but the bills keep arriving while I train.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who watches the children during classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My younger child is ten and Lina works late twice a week. I would choose a class on her early nights or wait for the next intake rather than leave the children alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would venues accept the certificate?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask venues whether they accept the certificate before enrolling. If they only want experienced sound engineers, I will not spend our mortgage money on the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the youth centre ten years is long enough to make a better plan for the children and the mortgage. I would still run a live session if people pay for it, even while I use the new tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, and robots that can handle live work follow around 2039. I cannot retire then, so I need reliable pay beyond editing; ten years to train helps, but the two weeks saved today still matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask two venues about live sound rates and enrol in a course only if a bursary covers fees, venues accept it and childcare fits. By 2036 I'll aim for six months of expenses saved from confirmed centre and any paid venue shifts; in the first year after AGI, I'll take sound shifts only if venues still offer paid hours and the pay covers travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious today, even with the long warning. If the sound work holds, I may feel better later, but I cannot spend future wages on this month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy equipment to get started?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not buy a mixing desk to chase the venue work. I would use the venues' gear and wait for a signed paid shift before paying for anything new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who helps decide whether the course is affordable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would show Lina the course costs and likely shift rates, then decide together. We have two children to get through school, and a heroic gamble with our home is not a plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because editing and client hours could fall before I qualify for anything else. A written centre schedule, clear credit union terms and paid vacancies I can actually reach would help our mortgage survive.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask what the children hear when we discuss shifts at supper. Our children know the difference between a confirmed booking and me saying I hope the centre calls.

headlineQuote: Our children know the difference between a confirmed booking and me saying I hope the centre calls.
portrait: Emeka is a **43-year-old** junior musician with secondary schooling, recording at a youth centre, teaching bass and playing café sets.
He uses **AI daily**, yet has only two weeks of savings, two school-age children and a mortgage with Lina.
He expects **editing and booking** hours to fall before robots reach live work three years after AGI.
He seeks **written shifts**, conditional care home openings and funded sound training that fits childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most because paid screen tasks could disappear before a second skill pays.
whatWouldHelp: A **centre schedule**, clear credit union terms and genuine paid vacancies would help protect the mortgage.
